title: Rumour Response Hub
tagline: Practical theory for managing misinformation, crowd dynamics, and psychological distress during high-pressure incidents.

modules.heading: Rumour Management
modules.summary: Rumours grow when information matters to people but reliable facts are missing, delayed, confusing, or distrusted.

theories.name: Allport & Postman — Basic Law of Rumour
theories.idea: Rumour intensity tends to increase when both importance and ambiguity are high: R ≈ i × a.
theories.use: Reduce ambiguity quickly with verified facts, clear timestamps, and explicit statements about what is still unknown.

theories.name: Information Vacuum
theories.idea: When official information is absent, people fill the gap with peer accounts, assumptions, and emotionally compelling explanations.
theories.use: Communicate early, even when the update is simply what is known, unknown, and being checked.

theories.name: Inoculation Theory
theories.idea: People can become more resistant to misleading claims when warned about likely manipulation techniques before exposure.
theories.use: Pre-bunk common false narratives and explain the tactic, not just the specific false claim.

checklist: Capture the exact claim before responding.
Separate verified facts, plausible but unverified information, and false information.
Identify the trusted source best placed to clarify the issue.
Publish a short correction with evidence and a timestamp.
Monitor whether the rumour changes form after the correction.

modules.heading: Crowd Control & Crowd Psychology
modules.summary: Crowds are not automatically irrational. Behaviour is strongly shaped by shared identity, perceived legitimacy, communication, environmental stress, and interactions with authorities.

theories.name: Elaborated Social Identity Model (ESIM)
theories.idea: Crowd behaviour can change when people come to see themselves as sharing a common identity, especially after experiences viewed as indiscriminate or illegitimate.
theories.use: Use differentiated, proportionate responses and communicate why restrictions or directions are necessary.

theories.name: Emergent Norm Theory
theories.idea: In unfamiliar situations, crowds may develop new local norms by observing influential behaviour and interpreting what others appear to accept.
theories.use: Make safe behaviour visible, easy, and socially reinforced through stewards, signage, and consistent instructions.

theories.name: Deindividuation — Historical Perspective
theories.idea: Older theories proposed that anonymity in crowds reduces self-awareness and restraint. Modern research treats this as incomplete and highly context-dependent.
theories.use: Do not assume a crowd is inherently dangerous. Assess actual behaviour, identities, pressures, and triggers.

checklist: Observe density, movement, bottlenecks, heat, noise, and visible distress.
Distinguish peaceful participants from individuals creating immediate risk.
Use clear instructions, reasons, routes, and realistic timeframes.
Preserve safe exits and avoid creating unnecessary compression points.
Escalate interventions only when necessary, proportionate, and lawful.

modules.heading: Psychological First Aid
modules.summary: PFA is humane, practical support for people affected by distressing events. It focuses on safety, calm, connection, practical needs, and access to further help rather than forcing people to recount the event.

theories.name: Look — Listen — Link
theories.idea: A widely used PFA structure: look for safety and urgent needs, listen respectfully to concerns, and link people with information, services, and social support.
theories.use: Start with immediate practical needs before attempting deeper emotional discussion.

theories.name: Hobfoll's Five Essential Elements
theories.idea: Post-disaster support should promote safety, calming, self- and community efficacy, connectedness, and hope.
theories.use: Design support environments and messages around these five protective conditions.

theories.name: Do No Harm
theories.idea: Support should respect dignity, culture, privacy, autonomy, and the person's own coping resources.
theories.use: Do not pressure someone to talk, diagnose them, make promises you cannot keep, or separate them from natural supports without good reason.

checklist: Check immediate safety, medical needs, and basic necessities.
Introduce yourself and ask what the person needs right now.
Listen without pressing for details or demanding an emotional account.
Offer accurate, simple information and practical choices.
Connect the person with family, community support, or professional services when appropriate.

principles.title: Be early
principles.text: Silence creates ambiguity. Provide verified updates before speculation becomes the default explanation.

principles.title: Be specific
principles.text: State what happened, where, when, what is confirmed, what is unknown, and when the next update will come.

principles.title: Be proportionate
principles.text: Respond to observed risk rather than assumptions about a group, crowd, or distressed individual.

principles.title: Protect dignity
principles.text: Good incident management reduces harm while preserving trust, autonomy, and humane treatment.

footer: Educational resource — adapt all operational actions to local law, organisational policy, and professional guidance.
